reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in genes of the TGF-beta signalling pathway, most often TGFBR1 and TGFBR2, and also SMAD3, TGFB2, and TGFB3
Characterised by arterial tortuosity and aneurysms that can affect the aorta and its branches well beyond the aortic root
The triad of arterial tortuosity, hypertelorism, and a bifid or broad uvula/cleft palate is a classic clinical clue
Aneurysms tend to dissect at smaller diameters and younger ages than in Marfan syndrome, so surveillance and surgical thresholds are more aggressive
Whole-arterial-tree imaging from head to pelvis is recommended because aneurysms are not confined to the aortic root
Ectopia lentis is characteristically absent, which helps distinguish it from Marfan syndrome
Craniofacial, skeletal, and cutaneous features overlap with Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, so genetic testing guides definitive classification
Management combines medical aortic protection (beta-blockers and/or angiotensin-receptor blockers), close imaging surveillance, and earlier prophylactic vascular surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Loeys-Dietz syndrome arises from variants that disturb transforming growth factor beta signalling within the vascular wall. Paradoxically, despite loss-of-function receptor variants, downstream TGF-beta signalling is upregulated, driving abnormal extracellular matrix remodelling and smooth-muscle cell dysfunction. The result is a fragile, tortuous arterial tree with a propensity to aneurysm formation and dissection throughout the aorta and its branches. The same signalling disturbance underlies the craniofacial, skeletal, and connective-tissue features, and the widespread vascular fragility explains the elevated risk of rupture at relatively small vessel diameters.
additionalDifferentials: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement
Head-to-pelvis CT or MR angiography to map arterial tortuosity and aneurysms
Molecular genetic testing of the TGF-beta pathway aortopathy gene panel
Slit-lamp examination to confirm absence of ectopia lentis and assess other ocular features
Cervical spine imaging for instability before intervention or anaesthesia
Skeletal review for scoliosis, pectus deformity, and club foot
redFlags: Acute severe chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting arterial dissection or rupture
Aneurysm growth or an aortic diameter reaching the individualised surgical threshold
Aneurysms in cerebral or visceral arteries detected on surveillance imaging
Signs of cervical spine instability, especially peri-operatively
Pregnancy complications given the heightened maternal dissection risk
reference.prognosis: Prognosis has improved substantially with recognition, aggressive imaging surveillance, medical aortic protection, and earlier surgery, but the widespread and aggressive arterial disease still carries meaningful risk of dissection and rupture. Outcomes vary with the causative gene and the extent of vascular involvement.
pitfalls: Applying Marfan aortic surgical thresholds, which are too conservative for Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Imaging only the aortic root and missing distal or branch-vessel aneurysms
Overlooking cervical spine instability before intubation or surgery
Confusing it with Marfan syndrome despite the absence of ectopia lentis
Underestimating the maternal vascular risk during pregnancy
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
